scenes.title: INTERSECT
scenes.narration: The INTERSECT operator returns only the rows that appear in both query result sets, giving you their common overlap.

scenes.title: How INTERSECT works
bullets: It keeps rows present in both the first and second query.
The result contains distinct rows only.
Both queries must match in column count and types.
scenes.narration: INTERSECT compares two result sets and keeps only the rows that occur in both of them. Like UNION, it returns distinct rows, so duplicates within the overlap are collapsed. The usual set operation rules apply, meaning both queries must agree on column count and compatible types.

scenes.title: Evaluating an intersection
steps: Compute the distinct rows of each
Keep rows found in both sets
scenes.narration: The engine runs both queries and considers the distinct rows each produces. It then keeps only the rows that appear in both sides. What comes back is the intersection, the common ground shared by the two result sets.

scenes.title: Customers who bought in both years
scenes.code:
SELECT customer_id
FROM orders_2024

INTERSECT

SELECT customer_id
FROM orders_2025;
scenes.narration: The first query lists everyone who ordered in twenty twenty four, and the second lists everyone who ordered in twenty twenty five. INTERSECT returns only the customer ids that show up in both lists. This is a clean way to find loyal customers who purchased in both years.

scenes.text: INTERSECT is supported by PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server, and modern SQLite. MySQL historically lacked it, so on older MySQL you emulate it with an INNER JOIN or IN subquery.
scenes.narration: Most major databases including PostgreSQL, Oracle, and SQL Server support INTERSECT directly. MySQL historically did not offer it, so on older versions you emulate the same result with an inner join or an IN subquery.
